newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Latam markets rocked by Brazil stock price dive.
newsitem.headline: Latam markets rocked by Brazil stock price dive.

text.p: Brazilian stock prices plummetted Friday sending shock waves across Latin American markets where traders sold heavily on concerns about the health of the region's largest economy.
From Mexico City to Buenos Aires stock and bond prices plunged after Sao Paulo's leading Bovespa stock index dropped over eight percent in early morning trade.
By mid-afternoon the Bovespa index recouped some lost ground and was trading at 11,094 points, down 5.4 percent on the day.

"The Bovespa is yanking us up and down like a yo-yo," said an exhausted floor trader at the Mexico bourse, who complained the local stock prices had followed the Brazilian stock index's rollercoaster ride all week.

Still, regional markets were holding out better than Brazil. Mexico's IPC stock index was down 1.8 percent and Argentina's blue-chip Merval stock index was off 1.7 percent in mid-afternoon trade. Traders across the region said investors were concerned Brazil was heading down the same path as several Asian emerging markets that were forced to devalue their currencies after they came under attack in the markets.
They suspect Brazil may become the next target of the currency traders, as the country's real currency is widely believed to be overvalued by up to 25 percent.
However, Brazil Central Bank authorities on Friday were categorical that no currency devaluation was in the works and stressed there was no pressure on local currency markets.
"We are in no way considering a currency devaluation. We already said so earlier this week," said a clearly irritated Central Bank spokeswoman in response to a Reuter question.
In Brazil, analysts viewed the drop in local stock prices as unrelated to fears of a devaluation and said they were confident the Brazilian economy was on firm ground.
They said the decline in the Bovespa index, which has dropped over 15 percent so far this week, was triggered by the panicked small-time investors.

Analysts said many of these had ploughed their life savings into the bolsa in the hope of riding an extraordinary bull rally that had driven stock prices up over 90 percent in the first six months of the year.

"These newcomers don't have the experience or expertise to stick it out with a volatile asset like stocks. They are getting out at the first sign of trouble," said Craig Barley, international manager at Rio de Janeiro's Banco Omega.

Traders said Brazilian currency markets were trading calmly and reported the country was receiving a robust dollar inflow. They said that, so far this month, net capital flows showed a surplus of $1.99 billion in the Brazilian commercial foreign exchange market.
